Full breakdown with sources at the link below.

If you find this useful, please share. It helps more people find data-driven immigration analysis.

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

13 — countries for which DHS Sec. Noem has tried to terminate Temporary Protected Status since Trump returned.

The Haiti case at SCOTUS is one front in a much wider effort. The ruling (expected June) will set precedent for 1M+ people across all TPS nationalities.

100 — detainees who joined a hunger strike at Moshannon Valley Processing Center, the largest ICE detention center in the Northeast.

Officials denied it happened. Lawyers say ~40 were put in solitary. GEO Group's contracts ($3M/month) expire in September.

780 — use-of-force incidents by ICE staff on detainees since Jan 2025, per internal DHS records obtained by @washingtonpost.

~1.5 incidents per day, inside facilities. In the same period, the detention oversight office was cut from 100+ staff to just 5.

79 — children documented by @ProPublica as harmed by tear gas or pepper spray from ICE/CBP during Trump's crackdown.

Verified through body cam footage, witness interviews, and legal records. Nearly 4x the figure cited in a recent congressional report.

75,500 — asylum cases hit with a motion to "pretermit" since an Oct 2025 BIA ruling.

Pretermit = case terminated before a judge ever hears the merits. Result: 17,500 deported to third countries, 24,000 with removal orders, 12,300 who abandoned their claims entirely.

Welcome to my weekly segment called This Week by the {Immigration} Numbers. I’ll highlight some of the main takeaways from the week’s news that you might have missed. This Week by the {Immigration} Numbers (May 8, 2026). 🧵

More on immigration court transparency and data access at austinkocher.substack.com 
Full Paper: ir.lawnet.fordham.edu/cgi/vi…

What Zhang's note doesn't resolve: whether courts will actually take up a constitutional challenge to Rule 5.2(c), or whether reform would come through the Judicial Conference's rulemaking process. Both paths are slow. In the meantime, the rule keeps operating as written.

Zhang proposes a narrow fix: keep access restrictions on administrative records only,where sensitive personal data like asylum histories are hardest to redact at scale and make all other immigration filings remotely accessible by default, same as any civil case.

The Intercept had to file legal motions with help from a law school clinic, a law firm, and the Reporters Committee just to track habeas cases involving detained student activists in 2025. Local newsrooms can't do that for every case of unknown news value.

Author DH. Zhang (Fordham Law, 2026) argues the rule violates the First Amendment because it singles out immigration cases by content restricting access not by how records are filed but what subject matter they concern. That's a content-based restriction under Reed v. Gilbert.

The rule is Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2(c). It restricts remote PACER access to immigration and Social Security cases by default. To read the filings, you have to go to the courthouse in person, hire a runner, or ask the judge to lift the restriction case by case.

A 2026 Fordham Law Review note argues that federal courts are blocking journalists from remotely accessing immigration case records online and that the rule doing it is likely unconstitutional. The rule has been in place since 2007. Most people have never heard of it.

Full story reported by Documented NY: documentedny.com/2026/05/05/… 

 My broader analysis of ICE detention trends and the data behind them is at austinkocher.substack.com

His case illustrates something the detention data can't fully capture: the procedural mechanisms ICE uses to keep people detained even after judicial release orders. A judge granted bond. ICE placed a stay. A second judge then denied relief. That's three separate decision points.

A lawsuit ultimately led to his release in early May 2026. Rep. Dan Goldman (D-NY) said 30 other people were released alongside Marrero through his office's triage center. Marrero's attorney is from Make the Road New York.

The original detention stemmed from a removal order issued in 2022 after Marrero missed a court date while in a rehabilitation program for alcohol addiction. Attorneys describe a missed court date during medical treatment as legally recognized "good cause" for non-appearance.

He was transferred through at least 5 detention facilities: New Jersey, Arizona, Texas, the Everglades facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," and finally Mississippi. He described being shackled at the ankles, waist, and wrists for up to 8 hours during transfers.

Allan Michael Marrero spent 150 days in ICE detention after being seized at a routine marriage-based green card interview at 26 Federal Plaza in NYC last November. He has no criminal history. A judge ordered his release in January. ICE stayed the order and kept him locked up.
